question: According to (Subfoveal Macular Photocoagulation Study), which of the following patients should receive an urgent argon laser: (Jeffery)

options.A: A 65 year old man with VA of 20/400 and subfoveal CNVM of 3 disc diameter.
options.B: An 85 year old woman with VA of 20/100 and subfoveal CNVM of 1 disc diameter.
options.C: A 65 year old woman with VA of 20/400 and subfoveal CNVM of 3 disc diameter.
options.D: A 65 year old man with VA of 20/100 and subfoveal CNVM of 3 disc diameter.

explanation: The Macular Photocoagulation Study subfoveal arm only supported laser for lesions within its size ceiling of about 3.5 disc AREAS with well-demarcated classic borders and vision in the 20/40 to 20/320 range, and the benefit was greatest for small lesions, because photocoagulating the fovea causes an immediate drop in acuity that only pays off later against the natural history. A lesion of 3 disc DIAMETERS is roughly 9 disc areas, far outside the treatable range, which eliminates options A, C and D and leaves the 1 disc diameter subfoveal membrane with 20/100 vision in option B. This is a historical item only: subfoveal thermal laser has been abandoned in favour of intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy, which preserves rather than destroys foveal tissue.

question: Regarding ocular TB. ONE FALSE:

options.C: Latent TB affects mainly the vessels.
options.D: INH challenging test may diagnose ocular TB.

explanation: Latent tuberculosis means viable but contained bacilli with no clinical or radiographic evidence of active disease anywhere, so it does not by definition 'affect the vessels'; the retinal vasculitis of presumed ocular TB, along with choroidal granulomas and serpiginous-like choroiditis, is a manifestation of active or immune-mediated ocular disease, and the tissue most often involved is the highly vascular choroid rather than the retinal vessels. The other statements are defensible: interferon-gamma release assays have good sensitivity and, unlike the tuberculin skin test, are unaffected by BCG vaccination; a person with latent TB is not infectious; and a therapeutic trial of antituberculous therapy with sustained improvement is used as supportive evidence for presumed ocular TB when direct proof is unobtainable. I am flagging this one as low confidence because option A is also attackable, since IGRAs cannot distinguish latent from active infection and are usually taught as more specific than sensitive.
reviewConcern: Genuinely ambiguous polarity: a defensible case can be made for A as the false statement.

question: Patient developed shallow AC, 24 hours posttrabeculectomy.ONE TRUE:

options.A: Plus power lens can reduce his hyperopia.
options.C: Flat AC with lens-corneal touch is an indication of surgery revision.

explanation: A flat anterior chamber with lens-corneal or iris-corneal touch (Spaeth grade 2 to 3) is a surgical emergency: contact threatens irreversible endothelial decompensation and permanent peripheral anterior synechiae, so the chamber must be reformed and the underlying leak, overfiltration or misdirection addressed rather than observed. Option B is wrong because malignant glaucoma is only one of several causes and is far from the commonest at 24 hours; overfiltration, a wound or bleb leak with a positive Seidel test, choroidal effusion and pupillary block all come first, and the differentiating feature is that aqueous misdirection presents with a shallow chamber and HIGH pressure, whereas leak and overfiltration give a shallow chamber with hypotony. Option A is muddled: forward lens-iris movement in a shallow chamber typically produces a MYOPIC shift, while hypotony with choroidal folds and a shortened globe produces hyperopia, and in either case a spectacle lens is a temporising refractive fix, not a management of the flat chamber.

question: According to Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial. ONE FALSE :

options.A: IV methylprednisolone doesn't change the visual outcome.
options.B: Oral prednisone hasten the symptoms, but doesn't decrease recurrence.
options.C: Optic neuritis patients can be left without treatment.
options.D: No need for MRI in the typical cases.

explanation: The single most durable lesson of the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial is that MRI IS needed, because the number of white matter lesions at presentation is the strongest predictor of conversion to multiple sclerosis (roughly a quarter with no lesions versus a large majority with two or more over 15 years) and it drives the decision about disease-modifying therapy; so saying no MRI is needed in typical cases is the false statement. The trial also showed that intravenous methylprednisolone followed by an oral taper speeds visual recovery but leaves the final acuity essentially unchanged, that untreated observation is an acceptable option for vision alone, and that oral prednisone in standard dose used ALONE was associated with a higher rate of recurrent optic neuritis, which is why that regimen is avoided. Option B is loosely worded but is not the intended false answer.

question: (Case scenario) a female patient, post refractive sx. c/o photophobia at the night. All are possible management except : (From Kenneith Wright)

options.B: Turn on interior reading light in car

explanation: Night-time glare, haloes and starbursts after keratorefractive surgery arise when the scotopic pupil dilates beyond the effective optical zone, so every legitimate remedy either shrinks the pupil or enlarges the zone. Weak miotics such as low-dose pilocarpine or brimonidine keep the pupil inside the treated zone, switching on the car's interior light raises ambient illumination and constricts the pupil, and a retreatment that enlarges the optical zone with a broader transition removes the mismatch at its source. Polarised lenses do the opposite of what is wanted at night: they cut light transmission, further dilating the pupil and worsening scotopic symptoms, and they are generally advised against for night driving, which makes option D the management that does not belong.

question: Regarding post PKP decrease visual acuity in a patient with aphakic bullous keratopathy. The most common cause for this decrease in VA is?
explanation: In eyes grafted for aphakic or pseudophakic bullous keratopathy, cystoid macular oedema is the commonest reason the vision disappoints even when the graft itself is crystal clear, because these eyes have already had complicated or older-generation cataract surgery with vitreous disturbance and chronic low-grade inflammation, and the transplant adds a fresh inflammatory insult. The practical corollary is to examine the macula with OCT before blaming the graft, and to treat with topical steroid and a nonsteroidal agent, adding acetazolamide or periocular steroid for refractory cases. Glaucoma is a genuine and frequent comorbidity in these eyes and uveitis contributes, but neither is the leading single cause of reduced acuity in this specific group.

question: amsler grid held at 33 cm measures how many degrees :
explanation: The standard Amsler chart is a 10 by 10 cm grid of 5 mm squares, and at the prescribed 33 cm reading distance each small square subtends 1 degree, so the whole chart covers the central 20 degrees of visual field, that is 10 degrees of eccentricity in every direction from the central fixation dot. That is the practical reason the test is worn with the reading correction and held at a fixed distance: change the distance and the angular subtense, and therefore the field being sampled, changes with it. Choosing 10 degrees is the common trap, since 10 degrees is the RADIUS of the tested field rather than its full extent.

question: In papilledema, one false?

options.B: Starts superiorly inferiorly nasally then temporally?
options.C: Goes away in weeks to months
options.D: High water marks indicates atrophic papilledema

explanation: High-water marks are the concentric chorioretinal folds and residual retinal pigment epithelial lines left at the outer limit reached by subretinal fluid from a previously swollen disc, so they are a marker of CHRONIC or resolved papilledema rather than a specific indicator of the atrophic end stage; postpapilledema optic atrophy is recognised instead by pallor, gliosis, disc drusen-like bodies and optociliary shunt vessels. The remaining statements are conventional teaching: papilledema can appear within hours when intracranial pressure rises abruptly, the swelling is described as involving the superior and inferior poles first, then nasal, with the temporal margin last (mirrored in the Frisen grades, where the halo has a temporal gap early), and once the pressure is normalised the disc typically settles over about six to eight weeks. This is a weak recall and my answer rests largely on elimination, hence the low confidence.
reviewConcern: Answer reached mainly by elimination; option D is arguably true and options B and C are each defensible as the intended false statement.

question: Systemic lymphoma is least likely associated:
explanation: Among ocular adnexal lymphomas, the conjunctival ones carry the lowest rate of concurrent or subsequent systemic disease; they are typically indolent extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphomas presenting as a salmon-pink patch that is often localised and controlled with radiotherapy alone. Eyelid lymphoma sits at the other end, with the highest association with systemic lymphoma and a greater share of aggressive histologies such as diffuse large B-cell and mantle cell, and orbital disease falls in between. Whatever the site, every patient still needs full systemic staging with imaging and haematology referral, since the site only shifts the prior probability rather than excluding dissemination.

question: A 4 year old child with a history of infantile ET surgically corrected at the age of 12 months has VA of 20/30 with both eyes open but only 20/60 when each eye is tested monocularly. The most likely reason is:
explanation: Better acuity with both eyes open than with either eye alone is the signature of manifest latent nystagmus, which is strongly associated with infantile esotropia and absent binocular fusion: occluding one eye triggers a jerk nystagmus with the fast phase toward the viewing eye, degrading monocular acuity, while binocular viewing damps it. The practical correction is to fog the non-tested eye with a high plus lens or a translucent occluder rather than to patch it, so that binocular viewing conditions and the damped nystagmus are preserved. Bilateral amblyopia would not improve when both eyes are opened, crowding refers to worse acuity for a line of letters than for isolated optotypes, and binocular summation improves acuity by only about one line, not the doubling of the minimum angle of resolution seen here.

question: Regarding the lens, all true except:

options.A: Zonular fibers are composed of collagen filaments that merge with the capsule.
options.B: Lens epithelium resides beneath the anterior and equatorial capsule.
options.C: Lens capsule is composed of basement membrane and stains positive

explanation: Zonular fibres are bundles of FIBRILLIN-rich elastic microfibrils, not collagen, which is why fibrillin-1 mutations in Marfan syndrome produce zonular weakness and superotemporal lens dislocation; they arise from the nonpigmented ciliary epithelium and insert into the lens capsule near the equator. Option B is true: the lens epithelium is a single cuboidal layer beneath the anterior and equatorial capsule only, with no epithelium posteriorly, which is why posterior capsule opacification requires cells to migrate from the equatorial bow. Option C is also true: the capsule is the thickest basement membrane in the body, composed largely of type IV collagen and laminin and staining strongly with periodic acid-Schiff.

question: Which of the following is NOT associated with granulomatous uveitis:
explanation: Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is classified as a NON-granulomatous anterior uveitis: its keratic precipitates are small to medium, stellate with fine fibrillar extensions, and scattered diffusely over the whole endothelium rather than forming mutton-fat deposits in Arlt's triangle, and posterior synechiae are characteristically absent. Sarcoidosis is the archetypal granulomatous uveitis with mutton-fat precipitates, Koeppe and Busacca iris nodules and candle-wax retinal exudates; brucellosis is likewise granulomatous; and herpetic uveitis may present either way, often with granulomatous precipitates accompanied by sectoral iris atrophy and raised intraocular pressure. The stellate precipitates of Fuchs are sometimes described as granulomatous-like in newer literature, but standard classification still places the condition in the non-granulomatous group.

question: The most common cranial nerve palsy associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma is:
explanation: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma spreads superiorly through the foramen lacerum into the petroclival region and cavernous sinus, where the abducens nerve has the longest and most exposed intracranial course, so a sixth nerve palsy is the commonest cranial neuropathy and is often the presenting sign in a patient whose nasal symptoms have been dismissed. Trigeminal involvement is the next most frequent and produces the classic numb cheek from maxillary division compression, but it trails the sixth. Facial and vestibulocochlear deficits occur late and usually reflect extensive skull base disease or treatment effect, and the ear symptom that actually brings these patients in is a conductive loss from a middle ear effusion rather than a true eighth nerve palsy.

question: The management of bleb leak includes all of the following EXCEPT:
explanation: Conservative management of a bleb leak is aqueous suppression to reduce flow through the defect, a prophylactic topical antibiotic against blebitis, a large-diameter bandage contact lens or symblepharon ring to tamponade the leak, and reduction or withdrawal of topical corticosteroid so the conjunctival epithelium can heal; if those fail, autologous blood injection, cyanoacrylate glue or surgical revision follow. What is applied mechanically is a pressure patch, since a loose or light patch does nothing to appose the leaking edges, which makes that the odd one out.
reviewConcern: This is a soft item. 'Light patch' may be a transcription of 'tight patch' or 'pressure patch', in which case all four options are legitimate management steps. The compiler's hint pointed to the bandage contact lens, which is unambiguously a standard treatment, so I have diverged from it.

question: Purtscher-like retinopathy has been associated with multiple clinical entities, including acute pancreatitis, pancreatic adenocarcinoma, renal failure, preeclampsia/HELLP Syndrome and childbirth, connective tissue disord

options.A: 33% of all lattice degeneration will develop RRD b.33% of all RRD has lattice degeneration
options.C: Need prophylactic retinopexy if present with retinal hole
options.D: Only treated if associated PVD makes break and traction over the edge

explanation: Lattice degeneration is common, present in something like 8 to 10 percent of the population, and the overwhelming majority of lattice eyes never detach, so a figure of a third progressing to rhegmatogenous detachment is far too high; the roughly one in three figure belongs to the converse statement, that about a quarter to a third of detachments occur in eyes with lattice. Prophylactic retinopexy for asymptomatic lattice, with or without atrophic round holes, has not been shown to reduce detachment risk in a phakic eye without other risk factors and is generally not advised. Treatment is indicated when a posterior vitreous detachment produces a symptomatic break with persistent vitreoretinal traction on its edge, which is the situation option D describes.

The stem is also entirely bleed-through text about Purtscher-like retinopathy and must be replaced with the real lattice degeneration stem.

question: Lens dislocation in homocystinuria is usually bilateral and in 60% of cases occurs in the inferior or nasal direction. AAO Q59: Regarding Retinoblastoma, all are true EXCEPT:

options.A: 2 mutations in ch 13 should be present
options.B: They are susceptible for other malignancies in the future
options.C: Certain classification is to determine the survival

explanation: Knudson's two-hit model requires both copies of RB1 at 13q14 to be inactivated before a retinoblastoma develops, and survivors of the heritable form carry that first hit in every cell, which is why they face a lifetime excess of second malignancies, particularly osteosarcoma, soft tissue sarcoma, melanoma and pinealoblastoma. What the ocular classifications do not predict is patient survival: Reese-Ellsworth was built to predict globe salvage after external beam radiotherapy and the International Classification of Retinoblastoma predicts eye preservation with chemoreduction. Survival is driven by extraocular extension, optic nerve invasion beyond the lamina cribrosa and metastasis, which is what the separate International Retinoblastoma Staging System addresses.

question: The primary action is extorsion; secondary actions are elevation and abduction. Kanski Q80: in lid laceration involving superior canaliculus one TRUE

options.B: After 72h from injury it's is not possible to repair because you cant localize the cut edges
options.C: Need to be repaired only if the inferior canaliculus is involved

explanation: Any canalicular laceration should be repaired if at all possible, with fine apposition of the pericanalicular tissue over a silicone stent; the upper canaliculus is not disposable, since a proportion of patients drain preferentially through it and an unrepaired upper system can leave epiphora and lid notching. Repair is ideally performed within 24 to 48 hours, but delayed repair days later remains feasible, because the cut medial edge can usually be identified by careful inspection under magnification, probing, or irrigating the opposite punctum until fluid or air appears at the cut end, so the claim that repair becomes impossible after 72 hours is far too absolute. Canalicular lacerations follow dog bites, hooks and blunt medial lid avulsion; they are not markers of fatal injury and they are certainly not repaired only when the lower canaliculus is also cut.
reviewConcern: The stem is preceded by bleed-through text about inferior oblique actions. This answer diverges from the compiler's hint of B, which overstates the Kanski timing advice as an absolute cut-off.

question: regarding intraocular drug, all true except :

options.A: disruption of blood aqueous barrier may lead to drug inactivity
options.B: can be actively transported via vitreous
options.C: pigmentation may bind to the drug and prolong its presence

explanation: Drug leaves the vitreous by two routes: anteriorly, diffusing into the posterior and then anterior chamber to exit with aqueous through the conventional outflow pathways, and posteriorly, across the retina and retinal pigment epithelium, a route that includes active transport of organic anions such as the penicillins. Trans-scleral movement is a minor pathway and is not the main route of elimination, which makes that the false statement. The other three hold up: melanin in the uvea and pigment epithelium binds many drugs and prolongs their intraocular residence, active outward transport across the retina is real, and breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier floods the eye with protein that binds drug and reduces the free, pharmacologically active fraction.
reviewConcern: This diverges from the compiler's hint of A. Option A's phrase 'drug inactivity' is loosely worded, so the item remains arguable.

question: In Case of open globe injury, regarding the corneal epithelial healing all of the following are true except :-

options.A: Miosis happen at the edge of the wound site?
options.C: Small ultraviolet light increase epithelium mitosis

explanation: Corneal epithelial healing runs through a latent phase, a migration phase and only then a proliferative phase: cells at the leading edge flatten, dissolve their hemidesmosomes and slide across the defect, and mitosis at that leading edge is actually suppressed while migration is under way, with proliferation occurring behind the front and at the limbal stem cell niche. That makes the claim about mitosis at the wound edge the false statement. Fibronectin deposited on the wound bed is a well-established promoter of epithelial adhesion, spreading and healing, low-dose ultraviolet exposure has long been described as stimulating epithelial mitosis while larger doses inhibit it, and adrenergic agents that raise intracellular cyclic AMP, epinephrine among them, retard epithelial migration and division.
reviewConcern: Option A is transcribed as 'Miosis' with a trailing question mark; if the original word was not 'mitosis' the meaning of the option changes.

question: Regarding the ERG which of the following is responsible of oscillatory movement?
explanation: Oscillatory potentials are the small high-frequency wavelets riding on the ascending limb of the b-wave, and they are generated in the inner plexiform layer, principally by amacrine cell feedback circuitry. They are among the earliest electroretinographic abnormalities in diabetic retinopathy and in central retinal vein occlusion, both inner retinal ischaemic conditions, which is the clinical reason to know them. The retinal pigment epithelium generates the c-wave and the light rise of the electro-oculogram, horizontal cells contribute to the slow PIII and to shaping the b-wave rather than to the oscillations, and ganglion cells are essentially silent on the full-field ERG, appearing instead in the pattern ERG and the photopic negative response.

question: While you refracting the patient you find him plano at 67 cm. what is the refraction of the patient?
explanation: Retinoscopy measures the eye's refraction relative to the examiner's position, so the dioptric value of the working distance must be subtracted from the gross finding. A working distance of 67 cm corresponds to 1.50 D; neutralising with no lens in the trial frame means the gross result is plano and the net refraction is minus 1.50 D. Answering plano ignores the working distance correction altogether, and a plus answer applies that correction in the wrong direction.
reviewConcern: The options are written without signs; the intended answer is minus 1.50 D.

question: which one of these is true regarding inflammation of meibomian gland :
explanation: The meibomian glands are modified sebaceous glands embedded in the tarsal plate, so obstruction of one and the sterile lipogranulomatous inflammation that follows is a chalazion, a firm, painless, deeply seated nodule best appreciated on lid eversion. An external hordeolum, the common stye, is an acute staphylococcal infection of the glands of Zeis or Moll at the lash line, superficial and pointing anteriorly through the skin. The meibomian counterpart of a stye is the internal hordeolum, an acute infection of the meibomian gland pointing through the tarsal conjunctiva, which is what distinguishes it from the chronic, non-infectious chalazion.

question: Which of the following statements is not correct about vortex veins:

options.A: There are usually about 4-7 in each eye.
options.B: They drain the venous system of the rerna.
options.C: They drain the venous system of the choroid and anterior uvea.
options.D: They are visible in posterior segment examinaron

explanation: The vortex veins drain the uveal venous circulation, meaning choroid, ciliary body and iris, and they exit through oblique scleral canals a few millimetres behind the equator, where their ampullae are readily seen on indirect ophthalmoscopy of the mid-periphery. The retina drains through the central retinal vein, which leaves the eye within the optic nerve, so the statement that vortex veins drain the retina is the incorrect one. There are typically four to seven, roughly one or two per quadrant, and their number and position matter surgically because scleral buckling or drainage of subretinal fluid close to an ampulla risks choroidal haemorrhage or effusion.

question: chemical burn( one is true):

options.A: chemical material with ph more than 7 mean acidic
options.C: the destrucron depend on PH rather than concentraron
options.D: bleach is a common cause of alkaline burn

explanation: Household bleach, sodium hypochlorite, has a pH around 11 to 12 and is one of the commoner domestic alkalis to reach the eye, alongside ammonia in cleaning products, lye in drain cleaner and lime in cement and plaster. The other options invert established facts: a pH above 7 is alkaline rather than acidic, and alkalis are more destructive than acids because they saponify cell membrane lipids and penetrate rapidly into stroma and anterior chamber, whereas acids coagulate surface protein and to some extent barricade themselves out. Severity depends on concentration, volume and contact time as well as pH, so setting pH against concentration is a false dichotomy.
reviewConcern: Option C is a live alternative if the examiners intended the teaching that pH predicts severity better than the identity of the agent, and some texts describe bleach as causing only mild ocular injury.

question: stromal collagen which is true:
explanation: The corneal stroma is built predominantly of type I collagen fibrils, with type V co-assembled into those fibrils to regulate their uniformly small diameter and type VI forming the filamentous network of the interfibrillar matrix; that uniform fibril diameter and regular lattice spacing, held by the proteoglycans, is what keeps the stroma transparent. Type IV is the basement membrane collagen of the epithelial and endothelial basal laminae, type VIII is the major collagen of Descemet membrane, and types II and III are cartilage and reticular collagens with no meaningful role in the normal adult stroma, which rules out the other three combinations.

question: about lens all true except:

options.A: lens transparency due to crystallin proren which is insoluble

explanation: Lens transparency depends on the crystallins being water-soluble and packed at very high concentration in short-range order, so that scattered light cancels by destructive interference; when they aggregate into high-molecular-weight water-insoluble complexes, light scatters and cataract results, which means calling the crystallins insoluble reverses the physiology. The other statements hold: the fetal nucleus carries an upright Y suture anteriorly and an inverted Y posteriorly, secondary lens fibres are generated throughout life from the epithelial cells at the equatorial bow, and the lens epithelium is a single cuboidal layer confined to the anterior surface beneath the capsule.

question: When to do screening of DM type 1:
explanation: Type 1 diabetes has a datable onset and clinically significant retinopathy essentially does not appear within the first five years, so the first dilated fundus examination is recommended five years after diagnosis, with annual review thereafter. Type 2 diabetes is the opposite case: the onset date is unknown and a substantial minority already have retinopathy when the diagnosis is made, so screening begins immediately. Examining a newly diagnosed type 1 patient yields nothing, and the paediatric caveat is worth remembering, since screening is generally deferred until the child is around ten years old or has entered puberty, whichever comes first.

question: Brown's syndrome which is false:
explanation: Brown syndrome is a restriction of elevation in adduction caused by a tight, short or non-sliding superior oblique tendon-trochlea complex; adduction itself is full, which makes 'mainly adduction defect' the false statement. The forced duction test is positive, demonstrating mechanical resistance to elevating the adducted eye, and that finding is what separates Brown syndrome from inferior oblique palsy, in which forced ductions are free. Acquired Brown syndrome from trauma, trochleitis or an inflammatory arthropathy reflects swelling of the tendon or its sheath at the trochlea, may be intermittent, and is sometimes accompanied by a palpable or audible click.

question: about Yoke muscles which is false combination:
explanation: Yoke muscles are the pair that carry the two eyes together into a given field of gaze, and the vertical pairings are right superior rectus with left inferior oblique, right inferior rectus with left superior oblique, right superior oblique with left inferior rectus, and right inferior oblique with left superior rectus. Pairing the right superior oblique with the left inferior oblique is therefore the false combination: the right superior oblique depresses the adducted right eye in down-and-left gaze, where its yoke is the left inferior rectus, while the left inferior oblique elevates the adducted left eye in up-and-right gaze, where its yoke is the right superior rectus. The remaining three combinations are correct, including the horizontal pair of right lateral rectus with left medial rectus for right gaze.

question: stereoacuity which is wrong:

options.B: the images fall on the fovea

explanation: Stereoacuity is by definition a binocular function: it depends on the small horizontal disparity between the two retinal images being fused by cortical binocular cells, so it cannot be measured with one eye occluded. Monocular depth cues (motion parallax, overlap, relative size, shading) remain available with one eye, but they are not stereopsis, and monocular clues are precisely what good stereo tests are designed to eliminate. Option B is essentially correct for fine stereopsis, which depends on images falling on or very near corresponding foveal points with only a slight disparity.

question: upper eyelid lateral lesion mostly metastesize to which group of lymph node:
explanation: Lymphatic drainage of the eyelids splits laterally and medially: the lateral two-thirds of the upper lid and the lateral third of the lower lid drain to the preauricular (superficial parotid) nodes, while the medial upper lid and medial two-thirds of the lower lid drain to the submandibular nodes. A lateral upper lid malignancy such as sebaceous or squamous carcinoma therefore seeds the preauricular/parotid basin first, which is why that region is palpated at every eyelid tumour visit and is the target of sentinel node mapping. Submental nodes drain the central lower lip and chin, not the eyelid, and cervical nodes are a second-echelon station reached only after the parotid or submandibular group.

question: which of the following associated with RB homer w rossete:
explanation: Homer Wright rosettes are rings of tumour cells surrounding a central tangle of neural filaments (neuropil) with no lumen, and they signify neuroblastic or neuronal differentiation; they are shared with neuroblastoma and medulloblastoma and are not specific to retinoblastoma. The lumen-containing Flexner-Wintersteiner rosette, whose central space is bounded by a terminal-bar apparatus, is the one that indicates photoreceptor differentiation and is far more characteristic of retinoblastoma, while fleurettes indicate the most advanced photoreceptor differentiation. Optic nerve and uveal extension are routes of tumour spread and high-risk histopathologic features; they are graded independently of rosette formation and have no defining relationship to any one rosette type.

question: scenario of a man with anisocoria, one larger with slugish reaction which is true:
explanation: When the anisocoria is greater in light and the larger pupil reacts poorly, the lesion is on the efferent parasympathetic side or in the iris itself, and all three listed entities produce exactly that picture. Adie tonic pupil gives a large pupil with a sluggish, segmental light reaction and light-near dissociation from postganglionic ciliary ganglion damage; traumatic sphincter rupture gives an irregular, poorly reacting pupil with sphincter tears visible on slit-lamp; third nerve palsy gives a dilated, poorly reactive pupil, usually with ptosis and a motility deficit. Because the stem gives only the pupil finding and no ptosis, motility, slit-lamp, or pharmacologic data, none of the three can be excluded, so all of the above is the correct choice.

question: all of the following are true association except
explanation: Alport syndrome is classically paired with ANTERIOR lenticonus, an axial conical bulge of the anterior lens surface caused by a defective type IV collagen lens capsule that is abnormally thin; the associated dot-and-fleck retinopathy completes the picture. Posterior lenticonus is the one seen in Lowe (oculocerebrorenal) syndrome and, most often, as an isolated sporadic unilateral finding in otherwise healthy children. The other three pairings are correct: myotonic dystrophy gives the polychromatic iridescent Christmas-tree cataract, Wilson disease gives the copper sunflower cataract, and amiodarone deposits whorl-like anterior subcapsular opacities in addition to its corneal verticillata.

question: Which of the following topical anesthetic is a long acting ester
explanation: Local anaesthetics divide by the linkage between the aromatic ring and the amine chain: esters have a single i in the name before the -caine, amides have two. Tetracaine is an ester and is the long-acting member of that family, with an onset of about a minute and surface anaesthesia lasting up to 20 minutes or more, which is why it stings more and is more epitheliotoxic than the alternatives. Proparacaine and cocaine are also esters but short to intermediate acting, and bupivacaine, although genuinely long-acting, is an AMIDE and is used for injection rather than as a topical agent, which makes it the classic trap in this item.

question: Which of the following is false about the conjunctiva:

options.B: Goblet cell are present in the conjunctival substantia propria
options.D: bulbar conjunctival is loosely adherent to episclera

explanation: Goblet cells are unicellular mucin-secreting glands that sit WITHIN the conjunctival epithelium, discharging MUC5AC directly onto the ocular surface; they are not found in the substantia propria, which is the underlying vascular connective tissue stroma. What does lie in the substantia propria are the accessory lacrimal glands of Krause (fornices) and Wolfring (tarsal border), so option C is true. Option A is true because goblet cell density is highest inferonasally, in the fornices and around the plica and caruncle, and option D is true because the bulbar conjunctiva is only loosely attached to the underlying episclera except at the limbus, which is what permits ballooning chemosis and conjunctival autograft harvesting.

question: Which is true about iron deposits in the cornea:

options.A: Fleisher ring is found at the cone of keratoconus.
options.B: Stocker's line is found at the edge of trabeculectomy blebs.
options.C: Ferry's line is found in front of ptryguim
options.D: Iron deposition in the cornea due to aging is Hanle's line

explanation: The Fleischer ring is epithelial iron encircling the base of the keratoconic cone, best seen with a cobalt blue filter, so option A is the true statement. The other three are deliberately scrambled: the Stocker line is the vertical iron line at the advancing head of a pterygium, the Ferry line is the iron line at the edge of a filtering bleb, and the age-related horizontal iron line at the junction of the upper two-thirds and lower third of the cornea is the Hudson-Stahli line, not any Hanle line. All of these deposits are ferritin within basal epithelial cells and share the same mechanism, iron pooling in the tear film where the surface contour is irregular and tear break-up is abnormal.

question: Optic chiasm relation, All true except:
explanation: The cavernous sinuses lie LATERAL to the chiasm and sella, not above it, so calling the chiasm inferior to the cavernous sinus is the false relation. The genuine relations are that the chiasm sits in the floor of the third ventricle just behind and below the lamina terminalis, above and slightly in front of the pituitary stalk and diaphragma sellae, and medial to the supraclinoid internal carotid arteries on each side. These relations explain the classic lesion patterns: a pituitary mass compresses from below producing superior bitemporal loss, while a carotid aneurysm compressing the chiasm laterally damages the uncrossed fibres and produces nasal field loss.

question: All true about retino blastoma except.

options.A: survival and vision depends on the initial presentation
options.B: The first tumour to describe the genetic of malignancy
options.C: Survival is 70% in low-middle income countries
options.D: NVI and shallow AC are associated with poor histopathology

explanation: The stark global inequality of retinoblastoma outcome is the teaching point: survival exceeds 95 to 99 percent in high-income countries with screening and early presentation, but falls dramatically in resource-poor settings, where children present late with proptosis and extraocular disease and mortality approaches or exceeds 50 percent, so quoting a comfortable 70 percent for low-income settings understates the problem. The other statements are sound: presenting stage drives both survival and globe or vision salvage, retinoblastoma is the prototype tumour for cancer genetics through Knudson's two-hit hypothesis and the cloning of RB1 as the first tumour suppressor gene, and clinical features such as iris neovascularisation, glaucoma and a shallow anterior chamber correlate with high-risk histopathology (massive choroidal invasion, postlaminar optic nerve invasion, anterior segment seeding). Note that recent multinational data put three-year survival near 80 percent in lower-middle-income and near 57 percent in low-income countries, so the exact figure in option C is arguable even though it remains the statement the examiner intended as false.

question: Regarding the optic nerve, which is FALSE

options.A: Upon entering the cranial fossa medial to internal carotid artery
options.B: Enters the cranial fossa with the ophthalmic artery
options.C: Fibers are more in fetal than adult
options.D: The longest course is in the cranium

explanation: The optic nerve's longest segment is the intraorbital one, roughly 25 to 30 mm for an orbit only about 18 mm deep, which is why the nerve runs a redundant sinuous course that permits proptosis and free eye movement; the intracranial segment is only about 10 mm and the intracanalicular part about 5 to 10 mm. The remaining statements are true: within the optic canal the nerve is accompanied by the ophthalmic artery (running inferolaterally in its dural sheath), and once intracranial it lies medial to the internal carotid artery as it approaches the chiasm. Fibre counts are indeed higher in fetal life, around 3.5 million axons at mid-gestation, pruned by apoptosis to roughly 1.2 million by birth and adulthood.

question: Regarding nerve fiber layer, all true except
explanation: The retinal nerve fibre layer is made of the unmyelinated AXONS OF RETINAL GANGLION CELLS, not of bipolar cells; bipolar cells are the intermediate neuron of the vertical pathway and their axons terminate in the inner plexiform layer, never leaving the eye. Those ganglion cell axons run in the RNFL, turn into the optic disc, become myelinated only after passing the lamina cribrosa, and continue as the optic nerve to the chiasm, so options A and B are acceptable descriptions of where the fibre bundles begin and end. Option D is true and clinically central: glaucoma damages these axons in an arcuate, bundle-respecting pattern, which is what RNFL thinning on OCT and the corresponding arcuate field defects measure.

question: all statement regarding benign intracranial hypertension are true EXEPT:

options.A: is typically found in young obese females
options.C: is associated with features of hydrocephalus on a CT scan
options.D: is associated with visual disturbances that can be improved with LP shunt

explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is defined in part by NORMAL neuroimaging: the ventricles are normal or slit-like, never hydrocephalic, and the presence of hydrocephalus or a mass sends you looking for a secondary cause instead. The supportive imaging signs are the opposite of hydrocephalus, namely an empty sella, flattened posterior globes, distended perioptic subarachnoid spaces and transverse sinus stenosis. The other statements hold: the classic patient is a young obese woman of childbearing age, chronic otitis or mastoiditis can cause otitic hydrocephalus through lateral sinus thrombosis, and CSF diversion by lumboperitoneal or ventriculoperitoneal shunt is a recognised option for progressive visual loss when medical therapy fails.

question: the FALSE statement of cephalosporine is:

options.B: cefuroxime is a third generation cephalosporine
options.C: these drugs are effective against gram negative bacilli
options.D: they are effective against B lactamase producing staphylococci

explanation: Cefuroxime is a SECOND generation cephalosporin, not a third; it is worth knowing precisely because intracameral cefuroxime is the agent used for endophthalmitis prophylaxis at the end of cataract surgery. Third generation agents are ceftriaxone, cefotaxime and ceftazidime, the last being the classic intravitreal partner for vancomycin because of its antipseudomonal cover. The other statements are correct: cephalosporins are bactericidal beta-lactams that inhibit cell wall cross-linking, gram-negative bacillary cover broadens as you move from first to third generation, and their relative stability to staphylococcal penicillinase is exactly what makes first generation agents such as cefazolin useful against methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus.

question: which of the following is true for perforating ocular injury:

options.B: has a single entrance wound only
options.D: the globe integrity is disrupted in tow place due to an entrance and exit site(through and through injury)

explanation: In the standardised BETT terminology a PERFORATING injury means the wall of the globe is breached in two places by the same object, with both an entrance and an exit wound, whereas a PENETRATING injury has an entrance wound only. A partial-thickness wound is a lamellar laceration and does not qualify as an open globe at all, and no injury has an exit wound without an entrance, so options A, B and C are all definitionally impossible. The distinction matters practically because perforating injuries carry a worse prognosis, with a posterior exit site that often requires delayed vitrectomy and a higher risk of proliferative vitreoretinopathy and retinal detachment.

question: In pregnancy uveitis , false ?
explanation: Mycophenolate mofetil is a recognised human teratogen, associated with a distinctive embryopathy of microtia, cleft lip and palate and ocular malformations plus first-trimester pregnancy loss, and it carries a pregnancy prevention programme requiring effective contraception and a washout of about six weeks before conception; it is therefore emphatically NOT safe in pregnancy. Methotrexate is likewise an abortifacient and teratogen and must be stopped months in advance, so option C is true. Corticosteroids remain the mainstay for uveitis in pregnancy, given locally or at the lowest effective systemic dose (prednisolone is largely inactivated by placental 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase), with azathioprine and, if needed, ciclosporin or anti-TNF agents as the accepted steroid-sparing options.

question: Peribulbar VS retrobulbar. TRUE:
explanation: The whole point of the peribulbar technique is that the needle stays outside the muscle cone and is kept short and shallow, so the risk of globe perforation, optic nerve injury, retrobulbar haemorrhage and brainstem anaesthesia from inadvertent optic nerve sheath injection is lower than with a retrobulbar block. The trade-offs run the other way for the other two options: because the anaesthetic must diffuse into the cone from outside, peribulbar blocks need a LARGER volume (typically 6 to 10 mL versus 3 to 5 mL) and have a SLOWER onset, often requiring a supplementary injection and a longer wait for akinesia. That is the standard comparison to remember whenever an exam contrasts the two blocks.

question: Regarding Sphenoid bone all true except

options.A: formanen rotundum is part of the lesser wing
options.B: Pterygoid canal is Medial to foramen rotundum

explanation: The foramen rotundum, which transmits the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve, lies in the GREATER wing of the sphenoid, alongside foramen ovale and foramen spinosum; the lesser wing carries the optic canal and forms the upper border of the superior orbital fissure. Option B is correct in that the pterygoid (vidian) canal, carrying the nerve of the pterygoid canal to the pterygopalatine fossa, lies medial and inferior to foramen rotundum. Option C is also correct: the body of the sphenoid articulates posteriorly with the basiocciput at the spheno-occipital synchondrosis, a joint that fuses in the late teens and is a landmark in skull base imaging and surgery.

question: Regarding Wavelength all true except:

options.A: it Changes with density of media

explanation: Wavelength is a DISTANCE, the spatial separation between two successive corresponding points such as crest to crest, so calling it the cycle of a waveform confuses it with frequency, which is the number of cycles passing a point per second. The other two statements are standard optics: wavelength and frequency are inversely related through the wave equation, and when light passes into an optically denser medium its speed falls while its frequency is invariant, so the wavelength shortens in proportion to the refractive index. That last point is the reason laser wavelengths are quoted in air or vacuum and why photon energy, which follows frequency, does not change as light crosses an interface.

question: factors which make the RPE attached. All true except.
explanation: There are no junctional complexes binding the retinal pigment epithelium to the photoreceptors; the apical junctional complex of the RPE joins neighbouring RPE cells to one another and forms the outer blood-retinal barrier, so it is not one of the forces holding the neurosensory retina down. The genuine adhesive forces are the interphotoreceptor matrix that ensheathes the outer segments and interdigitates with RPE microvilli, the active fluid transport (metabolic pump) of the RPE working with the oncotic pull of the choroid, the hydrostatic push of intraocular pressure, and the viscoelastic tamponade of the formed vitreous. Their loss is what makes hypotony, RPE pump failure and vitreous liquefaction predispose to detachment, and it is why silicone oil or gas tamponade substitutes for the vitreous surgically.

question: Adenovirus infection in human, one false:

options.D: 3 types: Epidemic Keratoconjumctivitis, Follicular conjunctivitis, Pharyngoconjunctival fever

explanation: Adenovirus is the single most COMMON cause of infectious conjunctivitis worldwide, so calling it an uncommon cause of ocular infection is the false statement. Its classic ocular syndromes are the three listed: epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (serotypes 8, 19, 37) with subepithelial infiltrates and preauricular adenopathy, pharyngoconjunctival fever (serotypes 3, 7) with fever and sore throat in children, and non-specific follicular conjunctivitis. Severe cases form inflammatory pseudomembranes and, less often, true membranes that bleed when peeled and can leave conjunctival scarring and symblepharon, so both B and C are legitimate features.

question: All of the followings regarding slit lamp examination are true except:

options.A: Direct illumination are used to detect gross pathology
options.B: Corneal section is seen by direct illumination
options.C: Slit beam is used to illuminate cornea from behind in scleral scatter

explanation: In sclerotic (scleral) scatter the beam is decentred onto the LIMBUS and the light is then trapped inside the cornea by total internal reflection, so the cornea is lit from within its own edge, not from behind; any opacity scatters that trapped light and glows against a dark pupil. Illumination from behind is retroillumination, which uses light returning from the iris or the fundus red reflex, and that is a genuinely useful way to see corneal guttae as dark refractile spots (though specular reflection with its beaten-metal appearance remains the classic technique for them), so option D is acceptable. Direct illumination, whether a wide diffuse beam for a gross survey or a narrow optic section for depth localisation, keeps the illuminated and observed areas coincident, so options A and B are also true as written.

question: Regarding Pinhole, which is false

options.C: When 2 mm or less impairs the image quality.

explanation: A pinhole degrades image quality once it becomes SMALLER than roughly 1 mm, not at 2 mm; the optimum clinical aperture is about 1.2 mm, which is the compromise between blur-circle reduction and diffraction. Above that size the pinhole admits too many peripheral rays and stops correcting refractive blur; below about 1 mm diffraction spreads the light and both acuity and brightness fall. The two true statements follow from the same geometry: narrowing the entrance pupil shrinks the blur circle, which increases depth of focus at the retina and depth of field in object space, which is also why a pinhole improves vision in refractive error and irregular astigmatism but not in macular or optic nerve disease.

question: Pic of haab stria in a 20 year old, what test would aid in the diagnosis ?
explanation: Haab striae are healed horizontal or concentric breaks in Descemet membrane caused by corneal stretching in infantile glaucoma, and the question is really asking how to confirm that the eye was buphthalmic in childhood. Axial length, which remains permanently elongated once the immature sclera has stretched, together with an enlarged corneal diameter, provides that evidence in a twenty year old and also separates Haab striae from forceps-related Descemet tears, which are typically unilateral, vertical or oblique, and occur in an eye of normal size. Pachymetry gives a corneal thickness that is variable and non-specific in these eyes. Anterior segment OCT and UBM will image the breaks and the angle anatomy but only confirm what is already visible at the slit lamp rather than establishing the underlying diagnosis.

question: Which electomagnatic radiation cause exfoliation syndrome :
explanation: Exfoliation syndrome, the modern name for pseudoexfoliation, has been linked epidemiologically to cumulative ultraviolet and sunlight exposure alongside latitude, altitude and the LOXL1 genotype, which is the association the question is most likely testing. The tempting alternative is infrared, which causes true exfoliation of the lens capsule, the lamellar delamination of the anterior capsule seen historically in glassblowers and furnace workers; if the writer meant that entity rather than exfoliation syndrome the answer would be infrared instead. X-rays cause radiation cataract and microwaves are associated with thermal lens injury, but neither produces exfoliative material.
reviewConcern: Genuinely split between ultraviolet (exfoliation syndrome) and infrared (true exfoliation of the lens capsule) depending on which entity the writer meant.

question: After eom sx he has decrease in palpebral fissure which was not there before the sx :
explanation: The superior rectus and the levator palpebrae superioris share a common embryological origin and are linked by fascial attachments, so surgery on one moves the other: resecting or advancing the superior rectus pulls the levator forward and downward and produces upper eyelid ptosis, narrowing the palpebral fissure. Recession of the superior rectus does the opposite and causes upper lid retraction. Inferior rectus recession is linked through the lower lid retractors to lower eyelid retraction, which widens rather than narrows the fissure, so option D is the reverse of what is described. A superior oblique tuck produces an iatrogenic Brown syndrome and an inferior oblique myectomy weakens extorsion and elevation in adduction; neither has an eyelid effect.

question: pic of child showing limited elevation of right eye :
explanation: Faced with a limited elevation the first task is to decide whether the problem is restrictive or paretic, and forced duction testing under anaesthesia is what answers that question, separating a tight inferior rectus, an entrapped orbital floor fracture or a fibrosis syndrome from a true monocular elevation deficiency. Only once the mechanism is known can the correct operation be chosen. The Knapp procedure, full-tendon transposition of the horizontal recti to the superior rectus, is the treatment for a genuine double elevator palsy with free forced ductions, so it presupposes the very test that is being asked about and cannot be the first step.

question: Picture of a patient with XT at primary position, limited adduction of the right eye with up shooting what's your diagnosis ?
explanation: Exotropia in primary position with limited adduction and relatively preserved abduction is Duane retraction syndrome type II, in which the lateral rectus receives aberrant innervation and co-contracts with the medial rectus on attempted adduction. That co-contraction tightens the globe against the lateral rectus and causes the vertical upshoot, sometimes called the leash phenomenon, along with globe retraction and fissure narrowing on adduction. Type I is the common variant with limited abduction and esotropia in primary position, so both options that name it are excluded by the exotropia. Bilateral inferior oblique overaction produces elevation in adduction but with normal horizontal ductions and no retraction, and would not limit adduction.

question: When you are measuring cyclo refraction for a child if you are near to the neutralization Point what do you notice ?

options.A: Reflex become wider and faster * (and brighter

explanation: As the retinoscopic reflex approaches neutrality it becomes brighter, fills the pupil more completely and moves faster, until at neutrality it flashes on and off across the whole pupil with no discernible direction of movement. Far from neutrality the opposite holds, the reflex is dim, narrow and slow, so option B describes moving away from rather than toward neutrality. Skew or oblique movement of the reflex indicates that the retinoscope streak is off the principal meridian in an astigmatic eye and tells you to rotate the streak, and is not a sign of approaching neutrality.

question: 30 y/o male notice progressive unilateral change of color, IOP 44mmHg on 4 anti glaucoma medications. What is the next step in management ?
explanation: An intraocular pressure of 44 mmHg on four topical agents means maximal medical therapy has already failed, and in a thirty year old with progressive damage the next step has to be incisional surgery rather than another temporising measure. Oral acetazolamide is useful as a short bridge while surgery is arranged but it is not a durable answer and its systemic burden is poorly tolerated long term. Laser trabeculoplasty performs badly in young patients and in secondary glaucomas, and it is relatively contraindicated where inflammation is part of the picture, so it is unlikely to buy much at this pressure. A glaucoma drainage device, or a trabeculectomy with antimetabolite if that were offered, is the appropriate definitive step.
reviewConcern: The stem is vague about what the unilateral colour change represents, so the underlying diagnosis is uncertain; the management principle for failed maximal medical therapy is what carries the answer.

question: 7 y/o boy k/c of VCK with corneal ulcer 4x4 mm with translucent base, on medication for long time with no improvement , What is the next best management ?
explanation: A shield ulcer in vernal keratoconjunctivitis with a translucent or whitish base has accumulated a plaque of mucus, fibrin and inflammatory debris over the exposed Bowman layer, and that plaque is itself a mechanical barrier that prevents epithelial cells from migrating across the defect. No amount of additional topical therapy will heal it while the plaque remains, which is exactly why the ulcer has failed to improve on prolonged medication, so debridement or superficial keratectomy of the base, combined with intensified anti-inflammatory treatment and often an amniotic membrane or bandage lens afterwards, is the correct next step. Tarsorrhaphy addresses exposure and neurotrophic failure, which is not the mechanism here, and phototherapeutic keratectomy is a disproportionate intervention for a plaque that lifts with a blade or spatula.

question: 35 y/o present after 3 months Hx of ocular trauma (pic. of gonioscopy showing hyphema) lOP 33 mmHg,What is the most appropriate next step in management ?
explanation: Three months after blunt trauma, persistent blood in the anterior chamber and angle with an IOP of 33 mm Hg points to a red-cell-related secondary glaucoma - ghost cell glaucoma from degenerated erythrocytes migrating forward from the vitreous, or a haemolytic picture - in which the trabecular meshwork is mechanically obstructed by cells and macrophages. Observation is not defensible at this pressure after this long, and pilocarpine is the wrong drug class: miotics do little for an obstructed meshwork and are relatively contraindicated after blunt trauma with angle recession because they can worsen outflow and stir up inflammation. Anterior chamber washout, with removal of the vitreous reservoir if that is the source, is the definitive step once medical therapy fails or the pressure has been this high for this long. In real practice aqueous suppressants would be started first, which is why this key should be read with caution.

question: 35 y/o male DM & HTN Pt. for a long time he is on insulin, 2 pack/day smoker for the past 10 years,OS BCVA 20/100 or 20/200 AC WNL Fundus exam showing localised Vit. Hg not showing the retina below it, no clinical sings
explanation: A spontaneous vitreous haemorrhage in a diabetic eye is proliferative disease until proved otherwise, since neovascular tissue bleeding into the vitreous is the only common diabetic mechanism; severe NPDR by definition has no new vessels and cannot bleed into the vitreous, and calling it idiopathic ignores the risk profile in front of you. High-risk PDR is a defined entity from the Diabetic Retinopathy Study - NVD of at least a quarter to a third of a disc area, any NVD with preretinal or vitreous haemorrhage, or NVE of at least half a disc area with haemorrhage - and establishing it requires visible neovascularisation. Because the blood obscures the retina and no new vessels are documented, the defensible label is PDR; the eye is followed with serial B-scan and given panretinal photocoagulation as soon as a view returns.
reviewConcern: Some examiners treat any vitreous haemorrhage in a diabetic as evidence of high-risk PDR, so option D is a live alternative.

question: Regarding prognosis of PAN, which of the following is true ?

options.A: Death with in 1 year of diagnosis
options.B: If treated 5-year survival is 50% (decrease the risk of relapse by 50%, AAO (
options.D: Steroids decrease the risk of relapse

explanation: Untreated polyarteritis nodosa carries a 5-year survival of roughly 13 percent, and corticosteroid treatment raises that to about half, with cyclophosphamide pushing it higher still. That makes the statement that treated patients have roughly a 50 percent 5-year survival the classic teaching figure. Death within a year of diagnosis describes only the most fulminant untreated cases rather than the rule, and ocular involvement is not itself the prognostic driver: renal, cardiac, gastrointestinal and central nervous system involvement are what determine survival in this vasculitis.

question: 3 prism diopter base out over the right eye , what is equivalent to it:

options.A: 2 pd bi od and 1pd bi os
options.B: 2 pd bo od and 1pd bi os
options.C: 1.5 pd bo od and 1.5 pd bi os

explanation: Prism before either eye acts on the vergence demand of the pair, so a required amount of base-out can be divided between the two eyes, and 3 prism dioptres base-out over the right eye is conventionally split as 1.5 base-out before each eye. Splitting is preferred because it halves the peripheral distortion, chromatic aberration, image displacement and cosmetic thickness that a single large prism produces. Base-in before the fellow eye would not be equivalent: base-out right combined with base-in left puts both bases toward the same side of space, giving a yoked or version prism that shifts both images together and leaves the vergence demand unchanged.

question: after an attack of VZV 2 month ago, pt came complaining of redness, photophobia and blurry vision in the eye of the same side. No epithelial defect What is your Treatment ?
explanation: Two months after herpes zoster ophthalmicus, redness, photophobia and blurred vision with an intact epithelium is the classic picture of zoster stromal keratitis or anterior uveitis, both immune-mediated and both treated with a topical corticosteroid such as prednisolone acetate on a slow taper, usually with oral antiviral cover in the earlier phase. Trifluridine and ganciclovir gel are directed at active epithelial viral replication, and trifluridine in particular is frankly toxic to the epithelium with prolonged use; there is no epithelial defect here to treat. Ciprofloxacin addresses bacterial keratitis, which does not fit an intact epithelium or this time course.

question: what is the most common cause of failure in treatment of herpetic ocular disease:
explanation: Aciclovir has an oral bioavailability of only about 10 to 20 percent, and topical antivirals penetrate the cornea poorly, so inadequate drug concentration at the target tissue, compounded by the five-times-daily dosing burden and the poor adherence that follows, is the usual reason herpetic ocular disease fails to respond. This is precisely why valaciclovir and famciclovir, with far better absorption, were developed. True antiviral resistance from thymidine kinase-deficient mutants is well described but rare outside immunocompromised hosts, hepatic clearance is not a limiting factor at standard doses, and allergy leads to drug discontinuation rather than to treatment failure.

question: Diabetic VH, normal B scan no TRD, what is the next step:
explanation: A diabetic vitreous haemorrhage with an attached retina on B-scan is followed rather than operated on: most such haemorrhages clear enough over weeks to allow panretinal photocoagulation, and serial ultrasound is what guards against tractional detachment developing behind the blood. Vitrectomy becomes the answer when the haemorrhage fails to clear, when ultrasound shows traction threatening or involving the macula, or in a type 1 diabetic with dense bilateral haemorrhage where earlier surgery has been shown to help. YAG hyaloidotomy is a technique for a discrete premacular subhyaloid haemorrhage, not for diffuse vitreous blood, and anti-VEGF may hasten clearing but is an adjunct rather than the defined next step.

question: pt reading through +14 reading glasses complain after 1 her form reading what the cause
explanation: A +14 add puts the reading material about 7 cm from the eyes, a convergence demand of roughly 30 prism dioptres, far beyond what almost anyone can sustain; worse, converging eyes look through the nasal part of a strong plus lens, which adds a base-out prismatic effect and increases the demand further. Fusion breaks down into a manifest exodeviation after sustained near work, which is why high-add low-vision readers are dispensed with base-in prism incorporated or with one eye occluded. Esophoria is the wrong direction, since the induced effect is a convergence burden rather than an excess of convergence, and diplopia is the symptom that follows the exodeviation rather than its cause.

question: keratoconus patient vision with glasses 20/40 started on RGP lens and his vision improved to distant 20/20 Patient now complaining his near vision was better with glasses What is the explanation of his near vision:

options.A: decrees vortex distant with CL (because of increased accommodative demand)
options.B: Base out prism effect of CL
options.C: Increase depth of perception with glasses

explanation: Moving a minus correction from the spectacle plane onto the cornea abolishes the vertex distance, and for a myope that increases the accommodative demand at near: the spectacle-corrected myope enjoys a reduced accommodative requirement which disappears in contact lenses. The same shift also removes the base-in prismatic help that minus spectacles provide when the eyes converge, so convergence demand rises too. A keratoconic moved into rigid gas permeable lenses therefore gains distance acuity from the regularised anterior surface while finding near work harder. A rigid lens does not induce base-out prism in this setting, and depth of focus is if anything better with the sharper retinal image the contact lens delivers.

question: a pt prefers CL over glasses, why?

options.A: Has severe strabismus with face turn

explanation: Contact lenses are the classical optical choice in congenital nystagmus: they move with the eye so the correction stays centred whatever the eye position, and lid and corneal contact appears to dampen the nystagmus through trigeminal afferent feedback, improving acuity beyond the purely refractive effect. Spectacles in a nystagmus patient with an eccentric null point force viewing through the lens periphery, adding prismatic and aberrational error. Ptosis is the one situation where spectacles are actually preferred, since a ptosis crutch mounts on the frame, and a face turn from strabismus is usually managed with prism or surgery rather than by changing lens modality.

question: A case of a slowly progressive proptosis, APD, asking what does MRI show (I remember that it was an optic nerve meningioma)?

options.B: Fusiform enlargement of kinking of optic nerve

explanation: Optic nerve sheath meningioma produces slowly progressive proptosis with early optic neuropathy and an afferent pupillary defect, and its imaging signature is thickening of the sheath around a normal calibre nerve, which on axial contrast enhanced images produces the tram track or rail track sign and on coronal images a doughnut of enhancement around the darker nerve. Fusiform enlargement with kinking or buckling of the nerve is the appearance of optic nerve glioma, which typically presents in a child, often with neurofibromatosis type 1, and expands the nerve itself rather than its sheath. The recall itself records that the case was a meningioma, which fits the adult slowly progressive presentation described.

question: Which of the following would affect the measurement of IOP by Goldmann Applanation Tonometer (GAT)?
explanation: Goldmann applanation rests on the Imbert Fick assumption of an average, thin, uniformly elastic cornea, so anything that changes corneal thickness, curvature, rigidity or surface regularity changes the reading. A corneal diameter over 14 mm means megalocornea or a buphthalmic eye, where the cornea is stretched, thinned and flatter than normal, and the measured pressure will be falsely low. An anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line is posterior embryotoxon, a purely peripheral angle finding at the termination of Descemet membrane, and it has no bearing on what happens when a 3.06 mm central applanation prism flattens the cornea. It is worth remembering that the same reasoning explains falsely high readings in thick or oedematous corneas and falsely low readings after myopic laser refractive surgery.

question: A Cardinal picture showing a narrowing of palpebral fissure of right eye with overshooting, what is most likely dx?
explanation: Narrowing of the palpebral fissure with globe retraction on attempted adduction, accompanied by an upshoot or downshoot from the leash phenomenon as the tight lateral rectus slips over the globe, is the hallmark of Duane retraction syndrome in any of its types. The type is defined by which duction is limited, and type 1, with limited abduction and relatively preserved adduction, accounts for roughly four fifths of cases, whereas type 2 with limited adduction is much rarer. Given that the stem describes the overshoot and gives no abduction or adduction detail, and given that the option naming the overshoot explicitly matches the described picture, type 1 is the answer.

question: An attached picture of a girl with a ?head tilt to left side with a limitation of gaze (Poor recall of which gaze is limited; adduction or abduction), asking what is the diagnosis?
explanation: An abnormal head posture in Duane syndrome is a face turn, not a tilt, and it is adopted towards the side of the affected eye when abduction is limited, because turning the face brings the eye into the field where fusion is possible. A left face turn therefore fits a left Duane type 1 with an abduction deficit, which is also the commonest form of the syndrome by a wide margin. Type 2, with limited adduction, is rare and drives the face turn to the opposite side.

question: 23 y/o with intermittent extropia with poor control with 45 pd at distant and at near 25. Refraction +2 , What is the next step in management:

question: Best method to measure IOP in patient who is post Lasik 6 weeks, but you did OCT and no fluid found in the interface?
explanation: After LASIK the central cornea is thinner and flatter, so Goldmann applanation systematically underestimates true intraocular pressure. The Perkins tonometer is simply a handheld Goldmann and obeys exactly the same Imbert Fick assumptions, so it carries the identical error and is not an improvement. The Tono Pen applanates a much smaller area, is less dependent on central corneal thickness and curvature, and can be used peripherally away from the ablation zone, which makes it the best of the three offered. The explicit statement that OCT shows no interface fluid is there to exclude interface fluid syndrome, in which a fluid pocket under the flap makes applanation readings falsely low even in an eye with dangerously high pressure.

question: Picture showing small pigmented lesion of the lower lid, you removed it, how will you repair the lower lid?
explanation: Lid margin reconstruction is decided by the proportion of the lid lost. Defects up to about a quarter to a third of the lid, and up to about a half in an older patient with lax tissue, are closed directly with a layered primary repair after freshening the margins, sometimes with lateral canthotomy and cantholysis to gain a few extra millimetres. A semicircular Tenzel flap is reserved for defects of roughly a third to two thirds, and larger losses need tarsoconjunctival or free tarsal grafts. question: Visual field defect in NAION?
explanation: Nonarteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy infarcts a sector of the prelaminar optic nerve head supplied by the short posterior ciliary circulation, and because the watershed usually falls horizontally the resulting defect is characteristically altitudinal, most often inferior, and typically begins as an inferonasal defect or nasal step that broadens into the altitudinal pattern. Option A is the answer because it names both the nasal step and the altitudinal defect, which is the combination taught and the pattern most often recorded in the large NAION series. Isolated arcuate defects are more typical of glaucomatous nerve fibre layer loss, and a pure central scotoma with early severe colour loss should raise suspicion of optic neuritis or a compressive or toxic optic neuropathy instead. Option C is only a partial description, since the inferonasal defect in NAION is usually the early stage of a defect that becomes frankly altitudinal.

question: Patient had trauma and ended with RD and you did PPV with perfluoropropane and patient has broken tooth and the dentist wants to use nitric oxide, for how long patient has to wait to treat his tooth?
explanation: Nitrous oxide diffuses into a closed intraocular gas bubble far faster than nitrogen diffuses out, so it expands the bubble and can produce a sudden dangerous rise in intraocular pressure with central retinal artery occlusion. The wait must therefore cover the whole life of the bubble, and perfluoropropane is the longest lasting of the routine tamponades, persisting for roughly two months. Eight weeks is the correct interval for perfluoropropane, whereas one to two weeks would be appropriate only for sulphur hexafluoride and around four weeks for perfluoroethane. Patients are given a wristband or card for exactly this reason, and the anaesthetist should be told so that an air oxygen technique is used if surgery cannot wait.

question: IOL of 0 power, in a myopic patient, what's the benefit of implant Vs leaving pt aphakic?

options.A: Less risk of RD with implantation

explanation: In an extremely axially myopic eye the calculated power may be zero or negative, and the reason to implant a plano lens rather than leave the eye aphakic is that the implant maintains a physical diaphragm between the anterior and posterior segments. Without an implant, and particularly once the posterior capsule is opened by YAG or is breached at surgery, vitreous moves forward and can touch the corneal endothelium, which is the mechanism of aphakic bullous keratopathy and endothelial decompensation. The barrier also helps preserve the blood aqueous barrier, so a case can be made for less cystoid macular oedema, but corneal endothelial protection is the effect most consistently cited for this scenario. Answer D is wrong because standard teaching does favour implantation even when no refractive power is needed, and retinal detachment risk in these eyes is driven by the axial length and the state of the capsule rather than by the presence of the optic.

question: Visual hallucinations patient had brought the visual field testing from another place the visual field showed homonymus field defect that respect the midline where is the site of the lesion
explanation: A homonymous defect that respects the vertical midline places the lesion behind the chiasm, and the combination of a homonymous field loss with visual hallucinations is the classic occipital picture, whether as release hallucinations in the blind hemifield or as simple unformed photopsias and geometric shapes from occipital cortex irritation. Temporal lobe lesions are the main alternative, since they produce formed hallucinations of faces and scenes, but their field defect is a superior homonymous quadrantanopia from the Meyer loop rather than a full hemianopia, and the stem does not describe formed imagery. Parietal lesions give an inferior quadrantanopia with visual inattention rather than hallucinations, and frontal lesions cause a gaze palsy rather than a homonymous field defect.

question: you're referacting a pt, then you had a wide with the movement beam?
explanation: This is the same item as the earlier retinoscopy recall. A wide, bright, fast with motion means the reflex is close to but has not yet crossed neutrality, so the far point sits just beyond the retinoscope. question: 30 y/o African american patient with hilar lymphadenopathy, presented with acute eye pain and photophobia. What is the content of the finding that is depicted in the photo?
explanation: A young Black patient with hilar lymphadenopathy and acute painful photophobic uveitis is sarcoidosis, and the photographed finding is almost certainly mutton fat keratic precipitates or an iris granuloma. Granulomatous deposits are made of epithelioid cells, which are transformed activated macrophages, together with multinucleated giant cells, and it is the epithelioid cell that defines granulomatous inflammation and separates it from the non granulomatous pattern. Lymphocytes and polymorphonuclear cells make up the small fine keratic precipitates of non granulomatous uveitis such as HLA B27 disease, and a pure polymorph answer would only fit a hypopyon. Macrophages is the closest wrong answer because it is a partial truth, but epithelioid cells is the specific term examiners are testing here.

question: Patient with right eye mild ptosis and miosis, and left hypertropia, where is the lesion?
explanation: Mild ptosis with miosis on the right is a right Horner syndrome, and a left hypertropia in this setting represents a left superior oblique palsy. The trochlear nerve is the only cranial nerve that decussates before leaving the brainstem, so a right-sided nuclear or fascicular fourth nerve lesion weakens the LEFT superior oblique, while the descending oculosympathetic tract runs immediately adjacent in the dorsal midbrain; Horner syndrome with a contralateral fourth nerve palsy is the classic localizing pair for the midbrain. Cavernous sinus is the tempting distractor, but there the sympathetic fibres on the carotid and the fourth nerve are on the same side, so the vertical deviation would be ipsilateral to the Horner, not crossed. The pons carries the sixth and seventh nerves rather than this combination, and an orbital lesion cannot produce a Horner syndrome at all since the sympathetics to the lid and pupil are already committed by that point.

question: You did refraction with Retinoscopy without lens, showed wide beam and fast (with) movement in all directions, What's the refraction?
explanation: In retinoscopy the reflex becomes brighter, wider and faster as you approach neutrality, and with motion means the far point lies beyond the retinoscope, so more plus is still needed. At a standard working distance of two thirds of a metre the eye is neutralised when the true refraction is about minus 1.50, so the refractive error that produces a fast, pupil filling with motion while still on the with side is roughly minus 1.00. Plano and plus 1.00 would also show with motion but the reflex would be narrower and slower because they are one and a half to two and a half dioptres from neutrality, and minus 2.00 would already have crossed neutrality into against motion at that working distance. The same reasoning holds at a half metre working distance, where minus 2.00 gives true neutrality rather than with motion, so minus 1.00 remains the best answer either way.
